text: When all the kings west of the Jordan heard the news — those in the hill country, in the lowlands, and along the whole coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon: the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites —
they banded together to make war on Joshua and Israel, with one accord.
But when the people of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai,
they resorted to a ruse of their own. They set out disguised as envoys, with worn-out sacks on their donkeys and old wineskins, cracked and patched together.
They wore worn-out sandals, mended, on their feet, and threadbare clothes, and all the bread they carried was dry and crumbling.
They came to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant land; now make a treaty with us."
But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live right among us. How then can we make a treaty with you?"
"We are your servants," they said to Joshua. And Joshua asked them, "Who are you, and where do you come from?"
They answered, "Your servants have come from a very distant land, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard the report of him and of everything he did in Egypt,
and everything he did to the two kings of the Amorites east of the Jordan — Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan, who ruled in Ashtaroth.
So our elders and all the people of our land said to us, 'Take provisions for the journey and go to meet them. Say to them: We are your servants; now make a treaty with us.'
This bread of ours was still warm when we packed it at home on the day we left to come to you. Now look at it — dry and crumbling.
These wineskins were new when we filled them, and now they are split open. And our clothes and sandals are worn out from the great length of the journey."
The men took some of their provisions, but they did not inquire of the LORD.
So Joshua made peace with them and entered into a covenant to let them live, and the leaders of the assembly confirmed it with an oath.
Three days after they had made the treaty with them, Israel learned that these people were their neighbors, living right among them.
So the Israelites set out and on the third day came to their towns: Gibeon, Kephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim.
But the Israelites did not attack them, because the leaders of the assembly had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. And the whole assembly grumbled against the leaders.
But all the leaders answered the whole assembly, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel; now we cannot touch them.
This is what we will do with them: we will let them live, so that no wrath comes upon us for breaking the oath we swore to them."
And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole assembly, just as the leaders had promised them.

versions.text: And the leaders said, "Let them live." So they became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole assembly, as the leaders had decided.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has "the leaders said to them" (i.e., to the assembly), which the current rendering drops. Also, כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבְּרוּ לָהֶם is "as the leaders had said/promised to them" rather than "decided," which imports a nuance not in the verb דבר.

text: Then Joshua summoned them and said, "Why did you deceive us by saying, 'We live far away from you,' while in fact you live right among us?
Now therefore you are under a curse: you will never cease to serve as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of my God."

They answered Joshua, "Your servants were clearly told how the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you the whole land and to destroy all its inhabitants before you. So we feared for our lives because of you, and that is why we did this.
We are now in your hands. Do to us whatever seems good and right to you."
So Joshua dealt with them accordingly: he saved them from the hand of the Israelites, and they did not kill them.
That day Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the assembly and for the altar of the LORD — as they still are to this day — at whatever place the LORD would choose.

versions.text: That day Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the assembly and for the altar of the LORD at the place he would choose — as they are to this day.
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew, "to this day" modifies the ongoing service at the altar and stands before the phrase about the chosen place; moving it to the very end blurs the sense and leaves "he would choose" hanging awkwardly for an oral reader.
